explain.right: A slice starts at the first index and stops before the second, so s[1:4] takes characters at 1, 2, 3 -> "ell".
explain.wrong: It doesn't include index 4 or index 0; the 'stop before the end index' rule is the same off-by-one as range.

items.q: `name = "  Sam  "`. A learner writes `name.strip()` on its own line, then prints `name`. What prints?
options: "  Sam  " — strings are immutable, so .strip() returns a new trimmed string and the original is unchanged

explain.right: Strings can't be changed in place; .strip() builds a new string you must capture: name = name.strip().
explain.wrong: Calling .strip() without reassigning throws the result away; name still holds the original with its spaces.

items.q: With `city = "London"` and `temp = 12`, which produces the text `London: 12C`?

explain.right: An f-string (prefix f) evaluates each {expression} and drops its value in, so f"{city}: {temp}C" gives London: 12C.
explain.wrong: Without the f prefix the braces stay literal, and plain words like city/temp aren't substituted at all.

explain.right: .split() with no argument breaks the string on whitespace into a list of words.
explain.wrong: It returns a list (not a string or tuple), and splits into separate words rather than one-item list.
